# Sundial and water clock (`sundial_water_clock`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by round_earth_size, geometry_proof
- Core idea: A sundial tells the time from the direction of a shadow. On a simple dial for equal hours the shadow-casting edge points at the celestial pole, that is, slopes towards the visible pole at an angle equal to the absolute latitude. Each dial is correct only for the latitude it was made for, and it shows local solar time, which varies from local mean solar time by up to about 16 minutes. A water clock measures time by water running through a small hole. Flow slows as the level falls. Calibrate unequal level marks on an outflow clock, or supply an inflow clock from a constant-level tank. The smallest readable interval depends on the scale and the steadiness of the flow or shadow.
- Pitfalls:
  - Vertical gnomon with equally spaced hour marks
  - Carrying a dial to another latitude (Rome used a looted Sicilian dial wrongly for about 99 years, according to Pliny)
  - Treating Greek or Roman seasonal hours as fixed lengths: daylight and darkness were each divided into twelve
  - Marking equal intervals on a straight-sided outflow vessel as if the flow stayed constant, or ignoring changes of flow in the cold
- History: egypt: c. 1500 BC shadow clocks; c. 1400 BC outflow water clock (Karnak, reign of Amenhotep III); mesopotamia: 2nd millennium BC – water clocks measured by weight of water; gnomon in use by c. 700 BC; china: gnomon observations from the 2nd millennium BC; inflow water clocks with compensating tanks by the Han; greece: 6th c. BC gnomon from Babylon (Herodotus); c. 270 BC Ctesibius' regulated water clock; c. 50 BC Tower of the Winds, Athens; rome: Pliny reports a tradition of a sundial dedicated by Papirius Cursor in 293 BC. Varro dates the first public dial near the Rostra to 263 BC, brought from Catina in Sicily. Scipio Nasica installed a public water clock during his censorship in 159 BC.; islamic: 1371 – Ibn al-Shatir's dial in Damascus with pole-pointing gnomon and equal hours; europe: 15th c. – pole-pointing dials become standard
- Read:
  - Pliny the Elder, Natural History VII.213–215
  - Vitruvius, De architectura IX.7–8
  - Gerhard Dohrn-van Rossum, History of the Hour: Clocks and Modern Temporal Orders (1996)
